title: Alphabet's $190 Billion AI Bet Faces Investor Test as Q2 Earnings Loom
excerpt: Google's parent reports Wednesday amid Gemini delays, key departures, and mounting pressure to prove massive data-center spending is paying off.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • Alphabet's Q2 earnings report is due, with capex guidance up over 100% year-on-year.
  • Delays in Gemini 3.5 Pro and key researcher departures have heightened investor concerns.
  • Cloud revenue is projected to grow 64% in Q2, but AI adoption needs to accelerate.
  • CEO Sundar Pichai faces significant scrutiny over Alphabet's AI strategy and spending.

  • Alphabet reports Q2 results on Wednesday with 2026 capex guidance at $180–190 billion, up over 100% year-on-year.
  • The delay of flagship Gemini 3.5 Pro and departures of key AI researchers have added to investor unease.
  • Cloud revenue is expected to have grown 64% in Q2, but analysts say enterprise AI adoption must accelerate to justify the spending.
  • CEO Sundar Pichai's full-stack AI strategy faces its most significant investor test yet.

Massive Spending Under the Microscope

Alphabet, Google's parent company, reports its second-quarter earnings on Wednesday facing the most intense scrutiny of its artificial intelligence strategy since the AI arms race began. The company has committed between $180 billion and $190 billion in capital expenditure for 2026 — roughly double what it spent last year — and completed a record $85 billion equity raise in June to fund the buildout.

https://x.com/michaeljburry/status/2079426924779343926

The stakes are personal for CEO Sundar Pichai, the Chennai-born executive who has staked Alphabet's future on a full-stack AI approach spanning custom tensor processing units, the Gemini model family, and a rapidly expanding cloud business. But two developments have clouded the picture heading into earnings week.

> **"Combined capital expenditure for Alphabet, Amazon, Meta, and Microsoft is expected to reach a record $715 billion in 2026, nearly three times the 2024 total."**

"Combined capital expenditure for Alphabet, Amazon, Meta, and Microsoft is expected to reach a record $715 billion in 2026, nearly three times the 2024 total."

First, Alphabet delayed the launch of Gemini 3.5 Pro, a flagship model built to compete in AI coding tools and agentic AI tasks, from its planned June release. Second, the company has lost high-profile researchers including Gemini co-lead Noam Shazeer and Nobel laureate John Jumper of Google DeepMind to competitors.

"AI infrastructure spending isn't going to pay off in the way investors are expecting if enterprise adoption doesn't accelerate."

— Rebecca Wetteman, CEO, Valoir

Cloud Growth Remains the Bright Spot

Analysts expect Alphabet to report revenue of roughly $117 billion for the quarter, up 21% year-on-year, with Google Cloud continuing to be the primary growth engine. Cloud sales are projected to have grown at a 64% clip, matching the first quarter's pace, buoyed by multi-billion-dollar deals to supply AI compute to clients including Meta Platforms and Anthropic.

Bank of America analyst Justin Post estimates cloud growth could reach 70%, driven by accelerating capacity expansion and Google's comparatively efficient capital spending through its own TPU silicon. The bank maintains a $430 price target on Alphabet and expects management could raise the full-year capex range by roughly 5% to as much as $200 billion.

"While Google is missing the boat on AI coding and that's a very real growing concern ... Google's strategy is all about the ecosystem," said Dave Wagner, portfolio manager at Aptus Capital Advisors.

The Capex Question Facing Big Tech

Alphabet's spending is part of a broader pattern. Combined capital expenditure for Alphabet, Amazon, Meta, and Microsoft is expected to reach a record $715 billion in 2026, nearly three times the 2024 total. But the question of diminishing returns is gaining traction. HSBC analysts have flagged concerns about customers turning to lower-cost AI models, and Chinese open-source alternatives are increasingly competitive with American offerings at a fraction of the cost.

Alphabet shares are down about 9% since late April but remain roughly 13% higher for the year, making it the second-best performer among the "Magnificent Seven" stocks. On Monday, shares rose 1.5% following a report that Google is developing a new custom chip, dubbed "Frozen v2," designed to run Gemini models more efficiently — a potential path to reining in long-term infrastructure costs.

What It Means for Indian Tech

Pichai's spending decisions ripple directly through India's technology sector. Google employs tens of thousands of engineers in Bangalore and Hyderabad, and its cloud expansion has fueled hiring across Indian AI startups that build on Google Cloud Platform. Any signal that the company is rethinking the pace of investment could affect hiring plans and the broader ecosystem of developers building on Gemini.

Investors and the diaspora alike will be watching Wednesday's earnings call closely — not just for the quarterly numbers, but for Pichai's commentary on whether the enormous bet is generating the returns needed to sustain it.
